chunks: Realistic inductor model and parasitics. The question: Draw a realistic circuit model for an inductor. What are the parasitics and where do they come from?
A real inductor is not just an ideal coil. The wire has resistance. The turns sit close together and act like a small capacitor. The core wastes some energy as heat.
A realistic model adds those extras to the ideal inductor, so you can predict where the part stops acting like an inductor.
Think of a garden hose that is supposed to be a perfect pipe. In real life the hose is slightly narrow, so it has some friction. It also bulges a little, so it stores some water.
A real inductor is the same: the ideal coil is the pipe, and the extras are the friction and the bulge.
The model is a simplification, since the extras are spread through the part, not sitting in separate lumps.
R s is the copper (DC resistance rising to AC resistance with frequency).
C w is in parallel with the whole winding, so at high frequency it provides a bypass path around the inductance. R p represents the core loss across the inductance proper.
DCR: the DC resistance of the wire, in series with the ideal inductor. Winding capacitance ( C w ): tiny capacitance between the turns, drawn in parallel with the coil.
Core loss: energy wasted in the magnetic core as heat, drawn as a resistor.
Self-resonant frequency (SRF): where L and C w resonate, f 0 equals 1 over (2 pi square root of LC w ) . Quality factor ( Q ): how good the inductor is, omega L over R .
Take a 10 microhenries inductor with 5 picofarads of winding capacitance. Below about 22 megahertz it acts like an inductor.
At about 22 megahertz the inductance and capacitance resonate (pass energy back and forth between them), and the impedance peaks. Above that, the part acts like a capacitor.

"The real inductor is the ideal L in series with winding resistance, DCR going up to ACR with frequency, with a parallel capacitance across the whole winding from turn-to-turn coupling, and a parallel resistor for core loss.
That gives a self-resonant frequency one over two pi root L C. Below it, it's an inductor; at it, the impedance peaks; above it, it's a capacitor.
A 10 microhenry coil with 5 picofarads resonates near 22 megahertz. It also saturates, so L drops at high current."
